Rise in tourist inflow 
*381.   DR. KARAN SINGH:t 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of TOURISM AND CULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether tourist inflow for seven month period ending August, 2005 is up 
by 15.6 per cent to 2.37 Million against 2.05 Million in corresponding period last 
year; 
(b) whether the annual tourist inflow has been around 2.3 Million till 2003; 
(c) whether with the current growth rate, the tourist inflow is likely to 
cross 4 Million mark in 2005; 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Dr. Karan Singh. 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
(d) what steps, Government propose to take, to improve other facilities in 
India so that tourist inflow is further improved; and 
(e) what concrete steps Government propose to take to provide security to 
foreign tourists and also hotel and other facilities in various parts of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF TOURISM 
(SHRIMATI RENUKA CHOWDHURY): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Foreign tourist arrivals to India during 2001, 2002 and 2003 was 2.54 
Million, 2.38 Million and 2.73 Million respectively. 
(c) Going by the growth of about 14% observed during the first 11 
months of the year 2005 over the same period of last year, it is expected that 
foreign tourist arrivals during 2005 may be around 3.8 Million. 
(d) Development of places of tourist interest is primarily the responsibility of the 
State Governments. However, Ministry of Tourism provides financial assistance to 
the State Governments for the projects which are prioritized in consultation with 
them every year under its various schemes. Further, in order to improve the 
tourist inflow into the country, various steps taken by the Government, 
include:— 
 
• Development of tourist spots under its various schemes of 
infrastructure development of tourist circuits and destinations; 
• Direct approach to the consumers through electronic and print media 
through the "Incredible India" Campaign; 
• Creation of World Class Collaterals; 
• Centralized Electronic Media Campaign; 
• Direct co-operative marketing with tour operators and wholesalers 
overseas; 
• Greater focus in the emerging markets, particularly in the region of 
China, North East Asia and South East Asia; 
2 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
• Participation in Trade Fairs & Exhibitions; 
• Optimizing Editorial PR and Publicity; 
• Use of Internet and Web Marketing; 
• Generating Tourist Publications; 
• Re-inforcing hospitality programmes including grant of air passages 
to invite media personnel and tour operators on familiarization tours to 
India to get first hand knowledge on various tourism products; 
• Launching of Road Shows in keysource markets of Europe; 
• Focusing on growth of hotel infrastructure particularly budget 
hotels; and 
• Enhancing connectivity through augmentation of air capacity and 
improving road infrastructure to major tourist attractions. 
(e) For the safety and security of tourists, the Government has deployed Police at 
the International Airport and important tourist centres. They have also been given 
orientation training in tourism related aspects. The Ministry of Tourism has 
advised all the State Governments/UTs to deploy Tourist Policy at all important 
tourist centres/destinations, and many States have deployed the Tourist Police 
Force in one form or another. The Ministry of Home Affairs have also been 
addressed in this regard. 
As regards hotels, all the States have been requested to allot maximum number 
of plots in the States for setting up of hotels. Ministry of Railways have been 
requested to set up 100 Railway Hotels of 100 capacity each at the surplus railway 
land to augment the hotel accommodation. Guidelines have been issued for 
approval of Guest Houses with the objectives of providing standardized 
accommodation to budget tourist, and to augment the hotel accommodation in 
the country. For providing basic facilities to tourists at tourist places like clean 
toilets, water supply, parking areas, etc, and also to improve tourism 
infrastructure in destinations/circuits, Ministry of Tourism has been providing 
financial assistance to the States on inter-se priority basis subject to availability 
of funds.

Sir, the tourist figures which the hon. Minister has given us, relate to tourist 
arrivals. Now, in Europe, for example, if somebody visits Spain for one day, it is

*382. SHRI T.S. BAJWA: Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be 
pleased to state:

(b) if so, the details thereof;

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HEAVY 
INDUSTRIES AND PUBLIC ENTERPRISES AND MINISTER OF STATE OF 
THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): 
(a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Irrigation being a State subject, schemes for water resources development 
for irrigation are conceived, planned and implemented by the State Governments. 
However, Government of India provides financial support under A ccelerated 
Irrigation Benefit Programme (AIBP) to State Governments. 
So far, 11 major/medium irrigation projects in Jammu and Kashmir have 
been cleared under the AIBP for crea tion of irrigation potential of 0.032 
million hectare. A sum of Rs. 113.45 crore has been released to the Government 
of Jammu and Kashmir under AIBP.

activities related to agriculture and food processing.

Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
New Opium Policy 
The licensing conditions for grant of opium cultivation have a clause on 
forewarning the farmers about the conditions for licence in the next crop year. 
Among the clauses of forewarning issued in the Licensing Conditions last year 
(for the crop year 2004-05), there was a stipulation that "cultivators who had 
tendered opium during the crop year 2004-05 which has been found to be of a 
consistency lower than 55 degree will be debarred from licence for the crop year 
2005-06." This forewarning clause has been incorporated into the opium policy 
for the current crop year 2005-06 
The clause has been introduced in view of the growing tendency of 
cultivators of tendering water mixed opium. Under this provision, those 
cultivators who tender opium of consistency lower than 55 degree have not been 
issued licence during the crop year 2005-06. 3767 out of 72480

It has been observed that during the past few years there has been an increasing 
trend in tendering 'water mixed' opium. The 'water mixed' opium is being tendered 
by some unscrupulous cultivators deliberately to substitute for the raw opium 
apparently diverted to illicit channels for manufacture of heroin in illicit, 
make-shift laboratories. It was, therefore, felt necessary to debar such 
cultivators from opium cultivation. The government benefits by ge tting better 
quality opium by curbing the tendency of cultivators to mix water with opium and 
by controlling possible diversion of the narcotic material.

Stamp duty on green market transactions 
*390. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI. Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government have received representation from the 
Association of National Stock Exchange Members of India (ANSEMI) stating that 
equal investors have to pay stamp duty twice on all green market transactions 
routed through terminals located outside Maharashtra; 
(b) if so, the details of other issues raised therein; 
(c) whether any intervention of his Ministry has prompted the State 
Government of Maharashtra to revise its earlier decision; 
(d) whether Government are aware that Maharashtra Government has decided 
to revise its earlier decision in this regard; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (e) Under the 
Constitution of India, Stamp Duties (but not including rates of stamp duty) falls under 
Entry 44 of the Concurrent List. The Central Government has powers to fix the rates 
of stamp duty in respect of 10 instruments specified in Entry 91 of the Union List, 
whereas States have the powers in respect of the remaining instruments by virtue of Entry 63 
of the State List. The revenue from stamp duty is collected and appropriated by the 
State in which it is leviable. The Indian Stamp Act, 1899, lays down the law 
relating to Stamps. 
The Government of Maharashtra made an amendment in the Bombay Stamp Act, 1958, 
through the Bombay Stamp (Amendment) Ordinance, 2005 (which has since been 
replaced by an Act of State Legislature), inter-alia, inserting Article 51A which provides 
that record of transactions (electronic or otherwise) effected by a trading member referred to in 
section 10B, shall be subject to rates of stamp duty specified in this Article. The effect of 
this amendment is that records of all transactions carried out in stock exchanges located 
in Maharashtra (like BSE and NSE) shall be subjected to stamp duty in Maharashtra, 
irrespective of where the brokers or the investors are looted. 
The Association of National Stock Exchange Members of India (ANMI) had made a 
representation to the Government of India, inter-alia, stating that the amendment made by 
"Government of Maharashtra amounts to extra-territorial application of law since NSE 
members are located in every State of India, that the provisions of Article 51A are 
ambiguous in the sense that they do not clearly specify as to which instrument or record of 
transactions (out of a number of records created during transactions) shall be liable to stamp 
duty, and also that it tries to circumvent the Central laws and seeks to levy a Security 
Transaction Tax, in the garb of stamp duty. 
The Government of India, Ministry of Finance, had taken up the matter with the 
Government of Maharashtra, requesting them to reconsider their decision, as the amendment 
made by the State Government may lead to inter-state jurisdictional disputes, lead to 
avoidable litigation, and adversely affect the national character of stock exchanges, 
thereby hampering development of capital market in the country. The Government 
of Maharashtra has informed that the matter is under their consideration and that the final 
decision is not yet taken. 
40 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
A writ petition has been filed before the Hon'ble Delhi High Court 
challenging the validity of the amendment.

affected both banks and their clients;

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) to (c) World Bank has brought out a report in 
December 2004 titled "Scaling up Access to Finance for India's Rural Poor". 
Certain observations have been made in the report regarding functioning of rural 
financial institutions in India including problems faced by rural poor relating to 
absence of flexible products & services, high transaction costs, insistence on 
collaterals and interest rate restrictions. Certain suggestions have been made 
including providing flexible products at competitive prices to rural poor, need for 
composite financial services, simplification of banking procedures, better staffing 
policies and door step banking, use of technology etc. Further, it has been 
suggested to revisit the policies on setting caps on interest rate on deposits and 
advances, priority sector lending, restructuring the RRBs and Rural Cooperative 
Banks, better regulation and supervision and active role of Government in facilitating 
rural finance markets. 
(d) and (e) Government and RBI constantly monitor the credit needs of 
different sectors of the economy and undertake corrective measures, whenever 
required, to ensure that adequate funds flow to Agriculture, Small & Medium 
Enterprises and such other important sectors. RBI has already

of India, the Central Sales Tax (CST) is levied by the Central Government by 
vitue for Entry 92A of the Union List, but the same is assigned to the States 
within which the tax is leviable, as per provisions of Article 269 of the Constitution 
of India. Thus, the State Governments benefit from the CST. 
(c) to (g) The Central Sales Tax, being an origin-based tax, is 
inconsistent with the concept of VAT and need to be phased out. The abolition 
of CST will result in revenue loss to the States. At his stage, it is not feasible to 
estimate revenue loss to each State due to abolition of CST. However, as per 
provisional figures furnished by the States, total 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
CST collection during 2004-05 was around Rs. 15,100 crores. The 
Empowered Committee of State Financ e Ministers (EC) is presently 
deliberating upon the issue of phasing out of the CST and is expected to make a 
recommendation to the Central Government. The EC is deliberating upon the 
various options for compensating the revenue loss on account of phasing out of 
CST including giving the States larger share/powers in respect of taxation of 
services. Once the EC finalise its recommendations, the Central Government 
will take a view in this matter.

THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): 
(a) Article 243G of the Constitution (73rd Amendment) Act, 1992 provides that the State 
Legislature may devolve powers and responsibilities upon Panchayats with respect to the 
implementation of Schemes for economic development and social justice as may be 
entrusted to them including those in relation to the matters listed in the Eleventh Schedule. 
This Schedule lists 29 matters. 
(b) and (c) As the Constitution provides that it is legislatures of States that will 
endow the Panchayati Raj Institutions with powers and authority, all the States 
covered by the 73rd Amendment Act, have devolved matters to them in varying 
measure. Effective devolution of functions would need to be accompanied by 
devolution of funds and functionaries to the Panchayati Raj Institutions in order to 
empower them to function as institutions of self government in accordance with the 
Constitutional mandate. In order to evolve a national consensus on the measures to be 
taken to strengthen Panchayati Raj and ensure that Panchayati Raj Institutions function 
as institutions of self-government as envisaged in Part IX of the Constitution, the 
Ministry of Panchayati

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
Raj convened Seven Round Tables of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj between July, 
2004 and December, 2004. At the Round Tables, about 150 points for action, covering 
18 dimensions of Panchayati Raj, were formulated by consensus, inter-alia, these 
cover points of action pertaining to both the Centre and the States, relating to the 
effective devolution of functions, funds and functionaries to Panchayats. At the Kolkata 
Round Table, it was agreed that while devolution must eventually comprise the entire range 
of subjects provided for in the State legislation in a time-bound manner, States may prioritize 
their devolution programme to ensure that for such functions as are prioritized, there is 
full and effective devolution in empowering PRIs as institutions of self-government in 
respect of these functions. To this end, the first step is identification of activities related 
to devolved functions for each tier of Panchayati Raj Institutions within a time-bound 
period. The next step should be the devolution of functionaries to the Panchayati Raj 
Institutions on the basis of the activities to be performed at each tier. The final step which 
would complete the cycle of devolution wlould consist in the devolution of finances 
commensurate with the activities to be performed at each level of the Panchayati Raj 
Institutions. 
A Council of State Ministers of Panchayati Raj under the Chairmanship of the Union 
Minister for Panchayati Raj has been constituted to review the implementation of the 
recommendations. The first meeting of the Council was held on 5th-6th August, 2005 at 
Kochi, Kerala. A Committee of Chief Secretaries of States and State Panchayati Raj 
Secretaries has also been constituted under the Chairmanship of the Union Secretary 
(Panchayati Raj) to monitor the progress on the implementation of the 150 
recommendations of the Seven Round Tables and the decisions of the Council of State 
Ministers of Panchayati Raj. Four review meetings of the Committee have so far been held in 
April, 2005, June, 2005, September, 2005, and November 2005. 
With a view to interacting with Panchayats and carrying out a review with the 
authorities concerned of the progress in implementing the points for action mutually 
agreed to in the Round Tables, a process of visiting the States and UTs at the level 
of Union Minister for Panchayati Raj has been initiated. Eight States have been 
covered so far. These include Karnataka, West Bengal, Uttaranchal, Haryana, 
Chhattisgarh, Orissa, Arunachal Pradesh and Rajasthan. Each visit is

Minister of the State concerned, laying out the points of action on which the

Confederation of Indian Industries (CII) are working together to facilitate building 
linkages between Panchayats, Industries and business to create Rural Business Hubs 
(RBH) in different blocks of the country on the lines of the successful Thai 
experience of One Tambon One Product (OTOP). Rural Business Hubs will be a 
Public-Private-Panchayat Partnership to produce/improve/refine goods from 
locally available resources to enable larger market access. A joint RBH Council, 
comprising representatives of the Government and CII and eminent individuals 
working in this area, has been constituted for monitoring the process and reviewing 
the actions. 
At the initial phase, only one product from one Block Panchayat of all the 
States will be selected for setting up of  RBH. The State Governments with the 
help of Panchayats and Cll will identify the potential product which will be promoted 
covering every facet starting from product development to sales, with the focus on 
creating value addition and securing better prices. In the 'second stage, a Task 
Force of key stakeholders and resource personnel will be set up for ensuring 
development of the RBH in a set time frame. The Task Force will envaluate the product 
and prepare strategy for ensuring quality, better pricing and market access. 
(c) This initiative of the Ministry of Panchayati Raj was initially limited to 
nine states, to start with, as the newly formed Ministry of Panchayati Raj was 
taking shape and there was a shortage of officers and staff to follow up. These 
States were selected on the basis of initial response and interest shown by the 
states. The initiative has since been extended to all States/UTs covered by Part 
IX of the Constitution. 
(d) and (e) The financing of Rural Business Hubs is envisaged as a business 
proposition on the public-private-panchayat-partnership principle which will be supported by 
such 'top-up' funds as may be available for the purpose. Assistance is also envisaged 
from specialized institutions like NABARD, SIDBI, the Institution of Engineers in 
the form of finance, professional and technical guidance to panchayats for identifying 
and setting up RBHs. 
(f) The process of setting up of RBHs has already begun with the signing of 
three Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) in the States of

MOUs have been finalized and signed to set up RBHs for Jatropha plantation and 
production of bio-diesel in Faridabad and Mewat Districts of Haryana and Dungarpur 
District of Rajasthan. Subsequent to  an advertisement in certain leading 
newspapers, over 150 responses have been received from Panchayati Raj Institutions

development of Bio-Fuels through Panchayats under the RBH initiative. The RBH

Statement 
ROUND TABLE OF ASIAN OIL MINISTERS 
SUMMARY OF CONCLUSIONS 
NEW DELHI, 25 NOVEMBER 2005 
Ministers and Heads of Delegation from the principal Asian oil and gas 
producing countries - the Russian Fe deration, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, 
Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan - met with the principal Asian oil and gas consuming 
countries - Japan, the Republic of Korea, China, Turkey and India at the invitation of His 
Excellency Shri mani Shankar Aiyar, Minister of Petroleum and Natural Gas, India, in 
New Delhi on 25 November 2005. 
Noting the conclusions of the January Round Table which had brought together the 
principal West Asian and South-east Asian producing countries with principal Asian 
consuming countries, participants in the November Round Table came to the following 
broad conclusions: 
(i) It was noted that Asia in the 21st century is emerging as the largest single 
supplier of oil and gas, as well as the fastest growing consumption centres in 
the world. 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
(ii) Regional cooperation in the Asian oil and gas economy must be pursued within 
the framework of global cooperation. In this context, they welcomed the 
forthcoming assumption by the co-chair of the Round Table, Russia, of the 
chairmanship of G-8, and expressed the hope that the concerns and views 
expressed in this Round Table would be factored into G-8 initiatives for Energy, 
Ecology and efficiency which Russia proposes to undertake. They also welcomed 
the Russian intention to associate important producers and import-intensive 
countries, including participants in the Round Table, in the deliberations of the 
expert groups that are expected to be set up by G-8. 
(iii) Participants noted with concern the recent volatility in international oil and gas 
prices and agreed that stable and reasonable prices would be in the interests of 
producers and consumers alike to ensure, on the one hand, that the growth 
prospects of consuming countries are not damaged and, on the other, that 
investment in producing countries is promoted. 
(iv) The need was recognised to study the possibility and feasibility of promoting 
and developing gas and oil interconnections through LNG and through trans-
national oil & gas pipelines within the Asian region for integrating energy 
markets, as well as improving the transportation infrastructure, In relation to 
the oil logistics, the Republic of Korea offered to make available crude and product 
storages. This too would be studied. This study could include the 
exploration of all alternative linkages by land and sea throughout Asia, 
including alternatives of linking the Caspian basin to countries in South Asia. 
To this end, the Indian proposal to initiate such a study, in association with 
participating countries, in particular the Republic of Korea which has proposed a 
working group to prepare a master plan, under the overall aegis of the 
International Energy Forum, was endorsed. The study will also take into 
account the suggestion made in one of the presentations to the Round Table of the 
possibility of establishing the proposed Asian Gas Grid Institute. 
152 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
mi) The Japanese proposal was endorsed to study the possibility of     
networking the countries of Central, South and East Asia and 
elsewhere with the Japanese initiative to promote a Sustainable 
and Flexible Energy System (SAFE). 
(vi) The importance of mutual cross-investment to reinforce mutual trade 
in oil and gas and associated downstream industry was emphasized 
as the optimal means of promoting stability, security and sustainability 
in the Asian oil and gas economy. It was emphasized that 
environment-friendly investment in upstream and downstream projects 
should be encouraged, that the investment climate should be improved 
to augment investment in the Asian oil and gas sector, and that Asian 
investment in Asian properties, including those in the Caspian region, 
be supported. Initiatives towards this end were welcomed. 
(vii) The significance of  transparency in access to all relevant data 
relating to reserves, demand, supply and investment was recognized, 
and the importance of predictability was emphasized as a key element 
of stability, security and sustainability in the Asian oil and gas 
economy, and, indeed, the world over. 
(viii) It was agreed that practical steps be taken bilaterally and regionally, 
as well as globally, for networking the knowledge-base of participating 
countries in the development of the Asian oil and gas sector and the 
energy economy in general In this context, the need to move towards 
the most optimal energy mix for each country and towards new and 
renewable energy sources was recognised as a priority for the Asian 
and global economy. 
(ix) It was further agreed that cooperation among participants in human 
resource development and training programmes would contribute an 
important element to the development of the Asian oil and gas economy. 
(x) Asian countries may consider joining hands to undertake joint 
ventures towards developing modern oil & gas facilities with the latest 
technology in the upstream and downstream sectors of the oil and gas 
economy of Asia and elsewhere. Such cooperation may be based on 
sound considerations of equality and mutual benefit, sincere mutual 
treatment, and enhanced communication aimed at benefiting all 
partners in a win-win spirit. 
153 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
(xi) Participants agreed that this Round Table offers a truly significant opportunity for 
Energy Ministers of energy-producing and energy-consuming countries in the 
region. Accordingly, to strengthen business ties, regional cooperation as well as 
global cooperation, and with a view to strengthening dialogue, cooperation 
and exchange among each other, participants agreed to meet one every two 
years and to keep the complementary fraternal Round Table of West and 
South-east Asian countries informed of their deliberations as also to inform 
itself of the proceedings of that Round Table. It was also agreed that this 
Round Table would not be to the detriment of the dialogue in other regional 
and global fora. 
(xii) The Round Table gratefully accepted the kind offer to Turkey to organise, 
with Azerbaijan as co-chair, the next meeting of the Round Table. 
(xiii) It was agreed that this Summary would be put to the next Round 
Table for final approval.

2999. SHRI LALIT SURI: Will th e Minister of PETROLEUM &

THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) LPG requirements are met by a combination of 
domestic production and imports. A temporary shortage of LPG emerged in September 
2005 on account of various factors. PSU production in the period April—September, 
2005 was 303 (Thousand Metric Tonne) TMT less than planned; Reliance Industries 
Ltd. (RIL) 
170 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
production was 190 TMT less than planned. In consequence, physical inventories with 
oil marketing companies (OMCs) declined from 333 TMT at the beginning of April,

Catalytic Cracker (FCC) unit at Jamnagar for maintenance work. Moreover, at just

Katrina on US refineries. All these factors put together upset the plans made by OMCs

reduced to only about 1.5% of the average monthly consumption of LPG. However, the 
backlog at the micro-level may vary from market to market on account of operational 
reasons.

requirements.

3032. SHRI SHAHID SIDDIQUI: Will  the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) what step his Ministry has taken to make rain water harvesting more 
popular; 
(b) how much subsidy is provided by the Ministry for implementing rain water 
harvesting schemes; and 
(c) what steps are being taken to bring these schemes closure to the common 
people, so that they may benefit from it? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) 'Water' being a State subject, it is 
primarily the responsibility of the concerned State Governments to take steps to make rain 
water harvesting more popular. However, the following steps have been taken by the 
Ministry of Water Resources to encourage rain water harvesting :- 
(i) Circulation of Manual/Guidelines on Artificial Recharge of Ground Water to the 
States/Union Territories to enable them to formulate area specific artificial 
recharge schemes to check the declining trend of ground water levels. 
(ii) Central Ministries/Departments of Railways, Defence, Posts, 
Telecommunications, Central Public works Department and National 
Highways Authority of India have been requested to provide roof top rain 
water harvesting structures in the buildings under their control. 
(iii) A Central Sector Scheme on Study of Recharge to Ground Water in the country 
was implemented during the IX Plan under which 165 demonstrative recharge 
projects were taken up. 
200 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) Central Ground Water Authority (CGWA) has issued directions to 
Ground Housing Societies, Institutes, Hotels, Industries, Farm Houses, 
etc., in the notified areas of Delhi, Faridabad, Gurgaon and Ghaziabad 
and other areas of National Capital Territory of Delhi where ground 
water table is below 8 meters fro m ground surface, to adopt rain 
water harvesting system. 
(v) Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) has provided technical 
guidance on rain water harvesting to various agencies, including State 
Government agencies, educational institutions, private 
entrepreneurs and individuals. 
(vi) An activity namely, "Demonstration of Rain Water Harvesting from Roof 
Tops and two toilets in Government schools in rural areas in various 
States through Community Based Organizations (CBOs)" was taken up 
during Fresh Water Year, 2003-04. Based on its success, more girls 
rural Government schools have been covered with roof top rain water 
harvesting projects, during 2004-05 and 2005-06. 
(b) Ministry of Water Resources is not operating any such scheme. 
However, under the Bhagidari scheme of Delhi Government, Delhi Jal Board 
provides financial assist ance upto 50% of the cost , subject to maximum of 
Rs. 50,000/- for rain water harvesting to Resident Welfare Associations/Group 
Housing Societies, Private recognized/Government Schools, Ins titutions, 
Industrial buildings, Hospitals, Charitable Institutions, NGO buildings etc., in areas 
of National Capital Territory, where rain water harvesting is feasible. 
(c) With a view to bring rain water harvesting schemes closer to 
common people, films on rain water harvesting in urban areas and rural areas 
have been produced for wide publicity among masses. Mass awareness 
programmes and training courses on rainwater harvesting and artificial recharge 
of ground water have been organized throughout the country involving 
Central/State Governments/Non-Government OrganizationsA/oluntary 
Organizations/Resident Welfar e Associations/ Educational 
Institutions/Industries and Individuals. Rain Water Harvesting campaign has also 
been launched keeping in view the various target groups. Publicity through print 
media, telecasting of spots on the television, broadcasting message on radio, 
holding of seminars, workshops, conferences, etc., have also been 
undertaken.

Cleaning of Rivers and Lakes 
3039. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PI LANIA: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that due to siltification, big rivers, lakes, 
dam reservoirs get chocked, which results in loss of water as well as floods; 
(b) if so, what is the estimate of Government regarding the quantum of loss 
per year; 
(c) whether Government have identified certain rivers/reservoirs/lakes etc. 
for desiltification; 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the schemes proposed to be 
undertaken; and 
(e) what steps Government propose to take to improve the scenario 
and to make it labour friendly? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI SONTOSH MOHAN DEV): (a) and (b) As per the 
report namely "Compendium on Silting of Reservoirs in the country (2001)" for 144 
reservoirs, the weighted average annual loss in grass storage due to desiltation has 
been found to be 0.44%. In addition, as per the report of the Multidisciplinary 
Committee (2002) constituted by the Ministry of Water Resources under the 
Chairmanship of Dr. B.K. Mrttal, former Chairman, Central Water Commission, 
siltation in rivers is not pronounced and alarming. The Third Minor Irrigation 
Census (2000-01) has mentioned that about 85,000 tanks and other storages 
are not in use predominantly due to siltation and other factors like lack of 
maintenance, encroachment, etc. 
211 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
(c) to (e) Following the report of Dr. Mittal Committee, the Ministry of 
Water Resources constituted a Select Group under the Chairmanship of 
Chairman, Central Water Commission in order to identify action points in this 
regard. The action points inter alia included identificaion of vulnerable reaches 
along rivers by State Government have subsequently been forwarded to the 
State Governments to take necessary action in this regard. Govt. of India has 
also approved a pilot scheme "National Project for Repair, Renovation and 
Restoration of Water Bodies Directly Linked to Agriculture" in 2004-05 for a 
sanctioned outlay of Rs. 300 Crores to be implemented during the remaining 
period of the X Five Year Plan. The obj ectives of the scheme are to restore 
the storage capacity and the irrigation potential of the water bodies. 
The Central Water Commission has published a study report on siltation 
of reservoirs in January 2001 under the title "Compendium on s ilting of 
reservoirs in India". The report has addressed the issue of siltation of reservoirs and 
desiltation measures including dredging operations etc. It has been concluded 
that a better alternative is to increase the storage capacity of reservoirs in due 
consideration of the sediment loads providing arrangements for flushing of silt in 
the design of the dam and its operation schedule, in case of the new ones and 
raising of the dams whether it is technically feasible.

Outflow of IIT graduates to foreign countries 
*365. SHRI S.M. LALJAN BASHA:  Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any plans to set up NTs in foreign 
countries; 
(b) whether it is a fact that a large number of IIT graduates migrate 
immediately after their studies at IITs; 
(c) the extent to which Government are thinking of encouraging such an 
outflow of the students; 
 
(d) whether the high cost of education at IITs being borne by 
Government is not helping the common man; and 
(e) if so, the steps Government would consider to find ways and means 
to ensure that IIT students work for the country at least for some time? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (e) Government has no plans at present to set up NT's in 
foreign countries. It is a fact that students from NTs do go abroad for higher 
studies/employment. However, record of students leaving the country is not 
maintained by the Ministry. In the present scenario of globalization and 
liberalization, the movement of technical personnel across the national 
boundaries is inevitable. Such an outflow is regulated by prevalent market 
forces internationally. 
Investment by the Government in IITs by way of rants-in-aid do help the 
common man. The free structure at present in place being subsidized one, ensure 
equity and access to quality higher education. The benefits of the contribution 
of IIT students trickle down to the common man in many ways such as 
creation of jobs, improvement in quality of life etc. The NTs also undertake 
sponsored research in significant areas of development of the Nation. They 
create and develop technologies, help in developing the infrastructure and 
economy of the nation which in turn creates jobs and raises the living 
standards.

Central University for KBK Region 
*366.   MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that during a meeting with him the Chief Minister of 
Orissa has made a proposal for setting up a Central University for the KBK 
region (undivided Kalahandi, Bolangirand Koraput Districts) of Orissa; 
(b) whether Government are aware that a Central University, in this most 
backward tribal dominated region, would go a long way in encouraging higher 
education among the tribals where the literacy rate is below 50 per cent; 
(c) if so, the status of the proposal; and 
(d) the time-frame within which a Central University would be set up in 
that region? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (d) While the meeting referred to in the question did 
take place recently, no formal proposal for setting up a Central University for the 
KBK region has been received from the State Government of Orissa. A Central 
University is established, inter-alia, to correct regional imbalances or to cover 
large gaps in the higher educational map of the country. There are 11 
recognised Universities (including two institutions Deemed to be Universities) in 
the State of Orissa. According to the available information, the Berhampur University 
and the Sambalapur University have jurisdication over the districts comprising the 
KBK region in Orissa. These two Universities together have affiliated 102 colleges 
located in the region. While there have been demands from various States, either for 
setting up of new Central Universities or for conversion of the existing State 
Universities into Central Universities, the present policy of the Government is to 
lay emphasis on consolidation and expansion of facilities in the existing 
Universities. In view of this, no proposal to set up a Central University for the 
KBK region is presently under consideration of the Government.

*368   SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: 
SHRI BALWANT ALIAS BAL APTE: 
Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Government of Maharashtra has sought Government's approval

EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) 
The Indian Green Building Council had organized a conference in

I. The Government should make it mandatory for buildings above 
20,000 sq. ft. to incorporate minimum green features. 
H. At the State levels, the Urban Development Authorities should come

*371.   DR. K. MALAISAMY: 
SHRI C. PERUMAL: 
Will the Minister of LAW AND JUSTICE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the law for adoption in force in the country is 
inadequate and is more parent-oriented rather than child-oriented, without taking care 
of the family environment of the adoptee; 
(b) in this context, whether there is a strong urge for comprehensive laws 
and training of judicial officers to deal with inter community adoptions; and

(a) to (c) The law relating to adoption amongst the Hindus is contained in the 
Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956. The other communities take 
recourse to the provisions of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 for the purpose 
of taking care of children as guardians. It is not correct to say that the law 
relating to adoption is more parent-oriented rather than child-oriented. The 
welfare of the children would be the paramount

consideration in the appointment of a guardian. At present, there is no general 
law of adoption in the country. The Government is examining as to whether a 
general law of adoption may be enacted.

*375. SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA : Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether provisions outlined in Master Plan-2021 for Delhi would help 
in providing solutions for the regularization of commercial activities in 
residential areas and additional dwelling units all over Delhi (especially in the 
Influence Zone along metro corridor) and unauthorized colonies; 
233 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
(b) if so, the details thereof and by when it would be notified; 
(c) whether Government have informed the Hon'ble Supreme Court and 
Delhi High Court about these proposals and status of Master Plan 2021 so that 
they could take into account the new developments while giving directions in 
these matters; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI S. JAIPAL 
REDDY): (a) and (b) Draft Master Plan for Delhi (MPD)-2021 has been 
prepared after intensive studies on various aspects, and keeping in view the 
socio-economic needs of the city with the perspective for the year 2021. 
In regard to commercial activity, the draft MPD-2021 envisages a five tier 
commercial hierarchy to accommoda te requirements of shopping, 
commercial offices and other services activities in an integrated manner for the 
population at various levels. Under the mixed use policy, the Draft Plan provides 
for allowing non-residential activities on ground floor in residential premises 
selectively, after taking into consideration the community needs, 
environmental impact and provision for safe and easy traffic circulation and 
parking requirements. 
In so far as the Influence Zone along Metro Corridors is concerned, the 
draft MPD-2021 proposes enhanced norms subject to preparation and approval 
of comprehensive integrated scheme. Regarding unauthorized colonies, the draft 
MPD-2021 proposes that regularization is to be done subject to the preparation 
of proper layout and service plans and submission to local bodies/DDA, to 
ensure that minimum necessary/ feasible  level of services and facilities are 
provided. 
The objections/suggestions received in response to the Public Notice issued 
by DDA in the Newspapers on 8.04.2005 have been referred to the Board of 
Enquiry and Hearing for consideration. Finalization of the draft Master Plan is 
a statutory process laid down in the Delhi Development Act 1957 and the 
rules framed thereunder. The Act does not prescribe any timeframe for 
finalization of the Plan. 
(c) and (d) The norms proposed in the draft MPD-2021, would be 
operative after Notification of the plan in accordance with the process laid 
234

down in the Delhi Development Act 1957. Till such time, the provisions of MPD-2021 
which had been notified on 01.08.1990 and amended from time to time, are applicable.

Plan.

Uniformity in Education 
*378.SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken a decision for 'One Nation-One 
Education' in the country and if so, the details thereof; 
(b) the States where this system would be initiated first and by when; 
(c) whether keeping in view the most thickly populated State of Uttar 
Pradesh, to what extent this system would be beneficial; and 
(d) the financial aid to be given to the State in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HUMAN RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRI 
ARJUN SINGH): (a) to (d) there is no concept like 'One Nation-One 
Education' in the National policy on Education. Education is in the 
Concurrent List and the State Governments are free to devise their 
approaches and plans for Education. It is expected that all their initiatives will be 
within the framework of National Policy on Education. The National policy on 
Education, 1986, as modified in 1992, envisaged a National System of 
Education based on the principles embodies in the Constitution. The concept of 
national System of Education implies that, up to a given level, all students, 
irrespective of caste, creed, location or sex have access to education of a 
comparable quality. The National System of Education envisages a common 
educational structure. The 10+2+3 st ructure has now been accepted in all 
parts of the country. The National System of Education also envisages a 
national curricula framework which contains a common core along with other 
components that are flexible. 
The Higher Education is governed by UGC and various regulatory 
agencies set up by various Ministri es. These agencies ensure uniform 
recognition of credentials and also quality. 
237 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
According to the parameters of Government of India schemes, the 
resources flow to the States and other agencies.

Population of tribals 
*380.SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister 
of TRIBAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state; 
(a) the tribal population in the country, State-wise and gender-wise; 
(b) the number of tribals who have been deprived of their land so far State-
wise; 
(c) the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the steps to be taken by Government to protect rights of the tribals? 
THE MINISTER OF TRIBAL AFFAIRS (SHRI P.R. KYNDIAH): (a) A 
Statement giving tribal population in the country, State-wise and gender-wise is 
given below. 
(b) to (d) Land and its management fall within the administrative 
jurisdiction of the respective States as provided under Entry No. 18 of State 
List (List II) of Seventh Schedule to the Constitution of India. The Central 
Government plays only a coordinating and advisory role in this regard. There 
is no Central Law on restoration of alienated tribal land. However, States with 
large tribal populations have enacted laws prohibiting alienation of tribal land and 
providing for restoration of alienated land. As per reports received from the 
States, 3.75 lakh cases were filed in various Courts comprising an area of 3.46 
lakh hectares, out of which 1.62 lakh cases were decided in favour of tribals and 
1.80 lakh hectares of alienated land have been restored to Schedueld Tribe 
persons. Cases covering 0.58 lakh hectares of land are still pending for disposal 
in various Courts. Data regarding State-wise number of tribals who have been 
deprived of their land in the State are not maintained in the Ministry. 
During 1999-2000, the Ministry of Rural Development had constituted an 
Expert Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri B.N. Yugandhar, IAS 
(Retd.), former Secretary (Rural Development) to look into the existing 
laws/regulations of alienation of tribal lands in the country and to draft a model 
law on the subject in consultation of tribal lands in the country and 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
to draft a model law on the subject in consultation with the States, National 
Commission for Scheduled Caste/Scheduled Tribes, Ministry of Welfare, etc. 
The Expert Committee has submitted a report, which contains 
recommendations relating to (i) Land and Rights of Scheduled Tribes, (ii) 
Legal Improvements for Enforcement of Land Rights, (iii) Model 
Legislation, (iv) Land Acquisition, Displacement and Rehabilitation, (v) 
Forest Rights of Scheduled Tribes, (vi) Administrative and Organisational 
Measures for Effective Implementation,  and (vii) Socio-Economic Measures. 
Copies of the Report have been sent to the State Governments and to concerned 
Central Ministries for necessary action. However, since land is a State subject, the 
responsibility of enacting necessary legislation as well as ensuring its 
implementation rests with the State Governments. 
The tenurial and access rights of forest dwelling scheduled tribes in respect 
of forest land which they have been traditionally inhabiting for ages have not 
been adequately recognised so far, resulting in historical injustice to them. In 
order to provide a legislative frame-work for recognition of forest rights of the 
forest dwelling Scheduled tribes, the Ministry of Tribal Affairs has introduced 
a "Scheduled Tribes (Recognition of Forest Rights) Bill, 2005" in Lok Sabha on 
13.12.2005. The Bill, when enacted, proposes to recognise the forest rights of 
the forest dwelling scheduled tribes including tenurial security, ownership of 
MFP and certain other rights.

Committees for cases of sexual harrassment 
2744. SHRI K. CHANDRAN PILLAI: Will the Minister of HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Supreme Court has directed to constitute committees to look into the 
cases of sexual harassment in both the Central and State Government departments; 
261 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
(b) if so, the details of the Committees constituted so far, State-wise; 
(c) whether Government have noticed any lapse by any departments in 
constituting such committees; and 
(d) if so, the details thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI KANTI SINGH): (a) The 
Supreme court, in the judgement delivered in August, 1997 in the case of Vishaka 
and Others Vs. State of Rajasthan and Others, laid down norms and guidelines to 
be followed by the employees or other responsible persons in the workplaces 
or other institutions to prevent or deter the commission of acts of sexual 
harassment and to provide the procedures for resolution, settlement or 
prosecution of acts of sexual harassment by taking all steps required, including 
setting up of complaints committee to redress the complaint made by the 
victim. 
(b) The matter falls in the purview of the State Governments. 
(c) and (d) The National Commission for Women (NCW) has informed that 
according to the information which b ecame available during the interactive 
meetings held by it since November, 2000 with various organizations 
including State Government Departments, complaints committees had not 
been formed in a number of cases. Th e committee which existed did not have 
50% reservation for women. 
In July, 2004 and again in May, 2005, the Department of Women and Child 
Development emphasized to all Central Ministries/Departments and State 
Governments and Union Territory Administrations the need to ensure the setting up 
of complaints committee as per the guidelines laid down in the Supreme Court's 
judgement and their proper functioning.

(b) A statement is enclosed (See below). 
(c) Funds under the Mission are not earmarked state-wise/city-wise. For accessing 
funds, cities are required to prepare 'City Development Plans' (CDPS) and 'Detailed 
Project Reports' (DPRS) and submit them for appraisal to the competent authorities

Statement 
Details of JNNURM and its objectives 
* The mission comprises two sub-missions, viz., Sub-Mission-I for Urban 
Infrastructure and Governance and sub-Mission-ll for basic Services for the 
Urban Poor. 
* The Mission provides focused attention to 63 select cities in different 
States. 
* For cities/towns not covered under the Mission, the Ministry of Urban 
Development has launched a scheme known as Urban Infrastructure 
Development Scheme for Small and Medium Towns (UIDSSMT) while the 
Ministry of Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation has formulated a scheme 
known as Integrated Housing and Slum Development Programme 
(IHSDP). 
* The following on-going schemes of the Ministries of Urban Development 
and Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation have been subsumed in 
JNNURM:— 
(i) Infrastructure Development in Mega cities. 
(ii) Integrated Development of Small & Medium Towns. 
(iii) Accelerated Urban Water Supply Programme. 
(iv) Urban Reform Incentive Fund 
* Provision of Central assistance is linked to implementation of 
certain mandatory as well as optional reforms at the State and 
ULB/Parastatal levels. 
392 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
* Implementation of all mandatory and optional reforms has to be completed 
during the Mission period of 7 years beginning from 2005-06. 
* Central assistance is in the form of 100% grant to be funded as Additional 
Central Assistance (ACA). 
* Cities have to prepare City Development Plans (CDPs) and Detailed 
Project Reports (DPRS). 
* 5% of the Central grant or actual requirement, whichever is less, is provided for 
preparation of City Development Plans, Detailed Project Reports, Capacity 
Building, Information, Education and Communication (IEC) activities 
etc. 
* Signing of Tripartite Memorandum of Agreement (MoA) by the State 
Governments and Urban Local Bodies/Parastatals with Central Government 
is a necessary condition to access Central funds. MoA should indicate 
commitments and milestones to be achieved in the implementation of reforms 
at the State & ULB/ Parastatals levels. 
*FINANCING PATTERN 
Depending upon population, geographical location of the cities and category to 
which a city belongs, fund is provided as indicated below:— 
(i) 35%/50%/80%/90% of the cost of projects would be funded by Govt. of 
India through 100% ACA and 
(ii) 65%/50%/20%/10% would be funded by State/ULBs/Financial Institutions. 
* Funds to be released in four installments. 
* First installment shall be released on signing of MoA and approval of City 
Development Plans (CDPs)/Detailed Project Reports (DPRs).

last one decade; and

EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) Yes

employment on Current Daily Status (CDS) basis, in the country as a whole has been

The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council Bill, 2005 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE (SHRI H.R. BHARDWAJ): 
Sir, I beg to move: 
"That the Bill to provide for the creation of Legislative Council for 
the State of Andhra Pradesh and for matters supplemental, 
incidental and consequential thereto, as passed by Lok Sabha, 
be taken into consideration. 
Sir, The Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council Bill, 2004, was 
introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16th December, 2004, and was passed 
by the Lok Sabha on 15th December, 2005. 
The Bill seeks to provide for the cr eation of Legislative Council in 
the legislature of the State of Andhra Pradesh for matters supplemental, 
incidental and consequential thereto. Article 169 of the Constitution of 
India provides that Parliament may by law provide, inter-alia, for the 
creation of the Legislative Council if  the Legislative Assembly of the 
State passes a resolution to that e ffect by majority of the total 
membership of the Assembly and by a majority of not less than two-
thirds of the members of the Assembly present and voting. The same 
article also contemplates that any such law may contain such 
supplemental, incidental, consequential provisions as Parliament may 
deem fit necessary. 
Sir, the Legislative Assembly of Andhra Pradesh had passed a 
resolution on 8th July, 2004 in terms of Article 169(1) of the 
Constitution for the creation of a Legislative Council in the State. In 
this connection, it may be submitted,  Sir, that the Legislative Council 
existed in the State of Andhra Pr adesh prior to 1985, which was 
abolished w.e.f. 1st June, 1985. Thereafter, on the basis of a resolution 
passed by the Andhra Pradesh Legislat ive Assembly for revival of the 
Legislative Council in the State, a Bill to the effect, containing a similar 
provision for the State of Tamil Nadu also, was introduced in 
454 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
the Rajya Sabha on 10.05.1990, and had been passed by that House 
on 28th May,  1995. 
This Bill, however, lapsed on the dissolution of the Ninth Lok 
Sabha, and the State of Andhra Pradesh, later, withdrew its request for 
the revival of the Council. The present Bill seeks to provide for 
creation of the Legislative Council in the State of Andhra Pradesh, with 
a total strength of ninety members, 31 of which are to be elected by the 
local authorities, eight each to be elected by the graduates and teachers 
constituencies; 31 by the Legislativ e Assembly; and, the remaining 
twelve are to be nominated by the Governor. The local authorities have 
been represented in the Legislative Council or the Municipal Corporation, 
Municipalities, Nagar Panchayats,  Cantonment Boards, Zilla Praja 
Parishads and Mandal Praja Parishads. The constitution of the Legislative 
Council is; therefore, the same as it  had existed prior to its abolition, 
except for the local bodies, constituting the local authorities' 
constituencies.

that Resolution as per its rules of procedure. In 1996, the State

interest rates. All I am trying to say is that I do not want to get down to this 
level of number-throwing. But, if these points are made and some of my 
colleagues are attempted to respond, I think, they are not responding without 
looking at figures. And, certainly, I don't believe anyone looks at figures more 
closely than my friend, Mr Jairam Ramesh, and anyone looks at them more 
scholarly than Dr. Arjun Sengupta. So, I think, these figures are there for 
everyone to see. Let us come to the subject as to how is economy doing. 
Without doubt, the five years or six years of reforms in the NDA did bring a 
considerable strength to certain aspects of the economy. I have said that 
several times. But the point is, it is a point which I think, all of us, as 
political leaders should realize, sooner than later, is that the kind of 
economic reforms that were espoused during that period appears 
unacceptable to the people of India. They want reforms. But, they want 
reforms with a human face. They want reforms. But, they want reforms 
with a greater emphasis on rural India. They want reforms. But, they want 
reforms with a greater emphasis on rural India. They want reforms. But, 
they want reforms with a greater bias towards outcomes and how it 
improves the daily life of an avera ge Indian. If there is a change in 
Chidambaram Mark-I to Chidambaram Mark-ll, it is because I have, in my 
own way through my own reading, in my own thinking and in my own 
reflection, evolved, and I am convinced, that reforms are not an end in itself, 
reforms are a mean to an end. Reforms are the means by which the 
lives of everyone in this country can be improved, especially the very poor 
and the very destitute. With that in mind, I am cautious. Why am I 
cautious? I am cautious for the very reasons which Mr. Sinha has 
mentioned. I am cautious because I don't know how the world interest rates 
will behave. I don't know how petroleum prices will behave. And, I don't 
believe Mani knows either. I don't know the impact of natural calamities. We 
seem to have a succession of natural calamities in the last twelve months, 
beginning with Tsunami, floods and cyclones. Therefore, although the 
577 

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
first half has projected a growth rate of 8.1 per cent, I am more cautious and I 
say growth would be over 7 per cent. When I say over 7 per cent, obviously, 
what I mean is that it will be somewhere between 7 per cent and 8 per cent. 
The performance of two sectors is rather sluggish and that is coal and 
electricity. They are linked. Since coal is not doing well, electricity is affected. 
We are, therefore, addressing the issues of coal and electricity. If coal and 
electricity achieve, as they promise they will by the end of the year, six per 
cent growth rate over the last year, then, I believe, economy can grow close 
to 7.5 per cent. I am bound to be cautious. Any one in my chair would also be 
cautious. I don't believe the growth rate is plateauing. I don't believe so. On the 
contrary, I believe, that some sectors are still growing at a very brisk rate. If 
coal and electricity catch up to what we Budgeted for in the beginning of the 
year as possible growth rates, I think, the growth rate will continue to increase. It is 
possible to raise the growth rate. How? Growth is a function of investment. 
It is also a function of efficiency. Bu t, primarily, growth is a function of 
investment. Our Government is different from the previous Government, in 
the sense, that it believes that we must enhance the public investment. I 
don't believe anyone, on this side, is against the private investment. All that 
we say is, while we encourage the private investment, we must enhance the 
public investment. Now, the public investment and the private investment, 
together, if we are able to enhance, I believe the growth rate can easily be ramped 
up to a level of 8 per cent. Now, what is the record? Sir, let us look at 1996-97 
and 1997-98, the famous Mark-I years. The public gross domestic investment 
was 7 per cent and 6.6 per cent of the GOP. But in the six years that 
followed between 1998-99 to 2003-04, the public gross domestic investment was— 
please remember in the two earlier years it was 7 and 6.6 per cent— and, I 
am giving the six years' figures for everybody to notice, 6.6, 6.9, 6.3, 6.2, 5.4 
and 5.6 per cent. This is the problem. What all my friends tell me here is, I 
share their view, 'accelerate public investment'. I do not know what the figures 
would be, when we come to 2004-05. But the effort is to enhance and 
increase public investment even while encouraging the private investment. 
Together, the public investment and the private investment, if they are sharply 
ramped up, I believe, can increase the growth rate. 
Now, Mr. Sinha says that there have virtually been no reforms in this 
578 

[20 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
country since we took over. That's a very sweeping charge. What is the 
definition of reforms? Now, if you say that the National Food for Work 
Programme is not a reform measure, I can only be sorry for you. Or, if 
you say that the National Rural Employment Guarantee Programme is 
not a reform measure, I can only be sorry for you. It may not be a reform 
in the sense that we understood early. But, surely, hunger poverty is 
something that we must fight. And, the National Rural Employment 
Guarantee Programme is intended to fight hunger poverty. And, if we 
succeed over three or four years to eliminate hunger poverty—we are 
not talking about income poverty; we are not talking about other aspects 
of poverty, for example, low literacy is a function of poverty, child marriage 
is a function of poverty, poor housing is a function of poverty, poor nutrition 
is a function of poverty, poor transport is a function of poverty—we will 
be addressing hunger poverty. And, I believe, and I sincerely believe, 
that the National Rural Employment Guarantee Programme, because it 
addresses hunger poverty, is a major initiative of this Government, and 
we are committed to implement it. Sir, if that is not a reform, then, what 
is a reform? VAT is the single most important tax reform that this country 
has undertaken during the last sevent y years. It is a major reform. A 
reform that you espoused but suddenly for reasons, political or otherwise, 
you would not come on board. Now, I am glad that the BJP Governments, 
in the States are coming on Board. They came and met me. The State 
Finance Ministers of the BJP Governments have promised to come on 
board on the 01st of April, 2006. I would urge my good friend, Mr. 
Yashwant Sinha, to use his influence in his party—I believe he still has 
a lot of influence in this party—to ensure that the BJP States come on 
board. And, that is a major reform. We can go on and on. It is wrong to 
say that his Government is not committed to reforms. This Government is 
committed to reforms, except that  the definition of 'reforms' has 
undergone a change. 
Sir, to say that the FRBM targets are not met, is accurate. But that, 
I think, is a very superficial criticism. You have to look at the FRBM 
targets on the basis of adjusted and unadjusted figures. These are given 
on page 25 of the Mid-Term Review. This year, after the Twelfth Finance 
Commission, there is a paradigm change. We no longer borrow for the 
States. The States have to borrow. Everything that the Central Government, 
now, gives is in the form of grants.

RAJYA SABHA [20 December, 2005] 
Bharat Nirman is not the hype of Indian Shining. Bharat Nirman is a 
business plan, and having drawn up a business plan, we are determined 
to fund it. The Prime Minister, on more than one occasion, and, as recently 
as last week, has expressed his determination to fund it. We will fund 
Bharat Nirman. For the current year, Bharat Nirman is fully funded. 
Sir, on PPP, Jairam raised a number of issues. On PPP, let me tell 
you, Sir, the PPP guidelines were formulated only in November, 2005. 
We have so far received, I think, eight or nine proposals for the PPP. I 
think, the meeting took place yest erday. I am sure, some of those 
proposals are being approved. As  and when they are approved and 
announced, we will certainly make them public or when there is an 
opportunity, I will come to this House. 
Sir, on agricultural credit, I have given you the figures. There is a 
problem of tenant farmers. Owner farmers are able to get credit, but the 
tenant farmers are finding it difficult to get credit, because there is no 
record, there is no acknowledgement of tenancy. The Record of Tenancy 
Rights Act, in most States, stands unimplemented. It used to be a major 
reform in the 1970s and 80s, but now no State is implementing the Tenancy 
Record Rights Act. Nevertheless, we have directed banks to form, what 
are called, joint liability groups among tenant farmers and ensure that 
tenant farmers also get a proportion of agricultural credit. It is not very 
good, but, I am confident that this year we will show improvement over 
last year, and, in future, more tenant farmers will get credit. Unfortunately, 
most small and medium farmers are tenant farmers. It is the owner farmer 
who gets credit. If he is a tenant farmer, there is some difficulty in getting 
credit. But I am addressing the issue. 
Finally, Sir, various issues can be dealt with. Hydrocarbon Tax 
Structure issue is being addressed by Dr. Rangrajan Committee. They 
have promised to give us the record, sometime, in January. If the Report 
comes in time, I am confident that we would be able to reflect it in a 
suitable way. 
Sir, my respectful submission is that the demands that we have asked 
for are very modest demands, i.e. cash outgoes of only Rs. 1,965 crores. 
I, therefore, request t he House to pass and return the Bill to the Lok
